chapters.title: Chapter 1: Why Working Capital Matters to an Investor

lessons.title: Working Capital Is Not Cash: What It Actually Measures

children.text: A company can report a rising net profit every quarter and still scramble to pay its suppliers on time. That is not an accounting error. It is working capital, and if you only read the profit and loss statement, you are missing the half of the balance sheet that decides whether a business can actually fund its own operations.

body.text: Working capital is not cash sitting in a bank account. It is the money tied up in a business's day-to-day operating cycle: in unsold inventory, in bills customers have not paid yet, and in the gap before suppliers get paid.

children.text: Where Working Capital Lives on the Balance Sheet

Every balance sheet splits assets and liabilities into two buckets: non-current (long term) and current (short term). Working capital is built entirely out of the current bucket: the assets and liabilities a company expects to convert to cash, or settle, within twelve months.

columns.label: Current Assets: What's Tied Up
points: Inventory: raw materials, work in progress, and finished goods
Trade receivables: money customers owe for goods already delivered
Short term investments and loans given

columns.label: Current Liabilities: What's Owed Soon
points: Trade payables: money owed to suppliers
Short term borrowings, including working capital loans and cash credit
Other current liabilities: accrued expenses and statutory dues
Current portion of long term debt

body.label: Net Working Capital
body.context: Positive means more is tied up in short term assets than is owed short term. Negative means suppliers and short term lenders are effectively funding part of the operating cycle, which is common and not automatically a red flag, as later lessons in this course will show.

children.text: Net Working Capital, Worked Through an Example

Pull up any listed company's balance sheet on screener.in and you will find these same line items, just with real numbers attached. Here is a worked example for a hypothetical mid-cap, NSE-listed auto components manufacturer, referred to here as Bharat Auto Components Ltd, using its FY24 balance sheet.

body.caption: Bharat Auto Components Ltd — Current Assets and Liabilities, FY24 (Rs crore, illustrative)

body.label: Net Working Capital (FY24)
body.context: ₹460 crore of current assets minus ₹320 crore of current liabilities.

body.text: ₹140 crore of net working capital does not mean the company has ₹140 crore sitting in a bank account it can spend today. Only the ₹45 crore cash and bank balances line is actual cash. The remaining ₹415 crore sits in inventory, trade receivables, and other current assets: value the company has already spent money to create or deliver, and is still waiting to convert into cash.

body.title: Classifying a Working Capital Loan
body.question: A company takes a one-year working capital loan from its bank to fund raw material purchases. Where does this loan sit on the balance sheet?
options: It does not appear on the balance sheet
body.explanation: A working capital loan with a tenure of one year or less is a short term borrowing, and short term borrowings sit under current liabilities. It is money the company owes back within twelve months, which is exactly why it counts against working capital rather than adding to it.

body.title: Try It Yourself on Screener.in
steps: Open any NSE or BSE listed company's page on screener.in and go to the Balance Sheet section.
Note the 'Other Assets' figure for the latest year; this is where current assets typically sit in screener.in's compact layout.
Cross-check the annual report if you need inventory and trade receivables broken out separately.
Find 'Trade Payables' and any short term 'Borrowings' reported for the same year.
Calculate Net Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities and compare it with the company's market capitalisation to get a sense of scale.

body.text: Do not treat the full 'current assets' figure on a balance sheet as a company's spendable cash cushion. A company can show ₹500 crore of current assets while holding almost no real cash, if that figure is dominated by receivables and inventory that take months to convert, or may not fully convert at all if a customer defaults or stock turns obsolete. The rest of this chapter unpacks exactly why that gap between working capital and actual spendable cash can widen even while profit is rising, and how to spot it before it becomes a liquidity problem.

points: Working capital is not a cash reserve. It is the net investment tied up in short term operating assets like inventory and receivables, minus what is owed to suppliers and short term lenders.
Net Working Capital = Current Assets − Current Liabilities. It comes straight off the balance sheet, not the profit and loss statement.
Only the 'cash and bank balances' line within current assets is actual spendable cash. Inventory and trade receivables are value waiting to become cash, not cash itself.
A rising net profit and a shrinking cash position can both be true at the same time. That gap is exactly what working capital analysis is built to catch.
